name: Plan 9
summary: A distributed operating system organized around per-process hierarchical namespaces, a uniform 9P file-service protocol, file-oriented resource servers, and selectively shared process resources.

features.name: Per-process local hierarchical namespace
features.description: Plan 9 processes assemble private name spaces with bind, mount, and unmount; union directories combine trees while retaining local lookup order and creation rules.
benefits: Lets each process or window construct a tailored view of local and remote services using ordinary path operations.
costs: Local composition and union lookup add ordering and lifecycle rules; a namespace view is contextual rather than a single global filesystem.

features.name: 9P file-service protocol
features.description: Plan 9 uses 9P transactions to authenticate, attach, walk, clone, open, read, write, and clunk file identifiers over local or network connections.
benefits: Gives files, devices, processes, and remote services a common byte-oriented protocol boundary.
costs: Protocol state and server-side fid lifecycle must be maintained, and file semantics may be less specialized than a dedicated service API.

features.name: File-oriented resource services
features.description: Plan 9 exposes resources such as devices, processes, network interfaces, and windows through file hierarchies served by kernel or user-level servers.
benefits: Allows clients to use common naming, protection, and I/O operations across heterogeneous resources.
costs: Services must preserve file-like semantics and may require user-level servers, caching, or translation layers.

features.name: Selective rfork resource sharing
features.description: The rfork model creates or modifies process resources according to flags controlling name space, environment, file descriptors, memory segments, and notes; rendezvous supplies a synchronization primitive.
benefits: Supports a single process class with configurable sharing and copying boundaries.
costs: Fine-grained sharing flags increase composition flexibility and make ownership and synchronization reasoning more demanding.

mathematical_views.question: How do bind, mount, union, and unmount operations compose a process-local path hierarchy?
assumptions: Directories and mounted services are typed tree nodes.
Lookup order and creation permissions are modeled explicitly while filesystem implementation details are abstracted.

mathematical_views.question: How does a client turn a connection into navigable, opened, and released remote file objects?
assumptions: The model abstracts authentication details and byte transport while retaining request lifecycle.

mathematical_views.question: Which process resources are shared, copied, or detached across rfork and synchronization operations?
assumptions: Rfork flags define resource transition choices.
The view separates kernel process creation from user-level language/runtime conventions.
